strengths: The paper addresses an identifiable research audience interested in classification with dense covariance matrices and diverging spikes. Sparsity of the whitened mean difference provides a useful alternative to sparsity of the discriminant direction.

The whitening-and-screening procedure is clearly described, and entrywise eigenspace perturbation bounds are a promising analytical tool. Retaining information outside the leading principal-component subspace is a useful methodological distinction.
The experimental design includes relevant competing classifiers, 200 Monte Carlo replications with standard deviations, and two gene-expression datasets with held-out test sets.
weaknesses: Necessary: The main consistency proof does not establish Theorem 3 as stated. The theorem claims almost-sure convergence of conditional risk under log(p)=o(n), whereas Section 8.4 concludes score convergence in probability under the stronger condition log(n)log(p)=o(n). The missing conditional-risk and almost-sure arguments must be supplied, or the theorem and corresponding introductory claims narrowed. The abstract should also state the fixed-support and nonvanishing minimum-signal assumptions.

Necessary: The QDA extension contains a false population reduction. Equation (5.9) discards coordinates outside the supports of the whitened means, although covariance differences can carry classification information there. For example, take u=(0,1,...,1)/sqrt(p−1), Σ1=I+p uuᵀ, Σ2=I+4p uuᵀ, μ1=e1, and μ2=2e1. These satisfy the stated QDA sparsity, coherence, and spike conditions, with A0={1}. The reduced score uses only Z1, while the Bayes rule additionally uses (uᵀZ)². Thus consistency for the reduced score cannot establish Theorem 6. This extension requires additional structural assumptions, a different procedure, or removal.

Necessary: Section 5.1 incorrectly asserts that Fisher's Gaussian LDA rule is Bayes optimal for general elliptical distributions with arbitrary class priors. With a common radial generator h, the likelihood-ratio boundary involves log h(q1)−log h(q2), where qi is the class-specific squared Mahalanobis distance. For unequal priors this generally does not reduce to Equation (1.1). Sub-Gaussian tails do not resolve this issue. Restrict the claim appropriately, for example to equal priors and a common decreasing radial generator, and revise the multiclass extension accordingly.

Necessary: The numerical results require reconciliation with the specified data-generating models. For Model 2, Equation (3.1) gives oracle errors of approximately 5.28%, 3.62%, 1.96%, 0.59%, and 0.020% across the five reported correlations; Table 3 instead remains around 5.3%. The discrepancy is far beyond the reported Monte Carlo uncertainty. Several entries also repeat exactly between the 0.70 and 0.80 columns of Tables 1–2. Audit the model descriptions, calculations, and tables before relying on the performance comparisons.

Necessary: Resolve the whitening estimator's eigenvalue convention. Section 2.3 defines Λ_hat as the full leading sample eigenvalues, but then adds σ_hat² again in D_hat=(Λ_hat+σ_hat²I)^(-1/2). This double-counts the noise contribution relative to the population decomposition. Make the estimator and corresponding proof identities consistent. Also distinguish the known-rank, hard-thresholding analysis from the experimental choices based on explained variance and cross-validation.

Necessary: Qualify the feature-count comparisons. A selected coordinate of W_hat Z generally combines many original variables, so selecting 12 whitened coordinates does not imply needing only 12 measured genes. The manuscript recognizes this distinction in Section 2, but its experimental conclusions repeatedly compare transformed-coordinate counts with raw-variable counts as model-size savings. Label these quantities explicitly and limit the interpretation accordingly.

Optional: Rank-selection sensitivity, simulations directly satisfying all theoretical assumptions, and repeated splits for the small real-data test sets would better characterize robustness. Copyediting would also improve readability. These improvements are secondary to the mathematical errors and numerical inconsistencies that currently prevent acceptance.
